paragraphs.text: A brick of [Sichuan border tea](sichuan-dark:definition) from [Ya'an](ya-an:where-it-is), made in 1980. It is a [dark tea](dark:definition) of mature leaf and red moss, the reddish stem and shoot pieces that come with the leaf. Coarse leaf was chosen on purpose: the tea had to survive months on the road to the Tibetan highlands and then be boiled for hours.

For about a thousand years Ya'an was where [tea for Tibet](ya-an:tibet-trade) began its journey. [Porters](sichuan-dark:tea-horse-road) carried the bricks on their backs to Kangding, because the mountain track was too steep for loaded horses, and from there the tea went on to Lhasa in exchange for horses. That trade is why a city known for the green tea of [Mengding Shan](ya-an:mengding-shan) is a dark tea place as well. Trucks on the new highway took over from the porters in the middle of the twentieth century, a few decades before this brick was made.

Bricks like this were made to be kept, and the trade values an [older brick](sichuan-dark:ageing) more. At forty-six years, what this one has become depends on how it was stored as much as on the years themselves.

brewing.text: From a brick, cake or basket, ease the leaf off along the edge or from the top with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole pieces give up their flavour steadily; crumbs release it all at once and cloud the cup. Break a few pieces from the edge of the brick, rinse them with boiling water and pour that off at once. Then use boiling water and plenty of leaf. The leaf is coarse and gives up its flavour slowly, so people brew it two ways. Some steep it in short gongfu pours, a little longer each time. Others use long steeps while the pot is still hot, or simmer the leaf for several minutes in a pot, which is the traditional way on the plateau.

notice.text: A redder, browner liquor, a rounder body and a medicinal edge, often with wood and a dark sweetness.

unsupported.sentence: Bricks like this were made to be kept, and the trade values an older brick more.
unsupported.why: The ageing claim says only that Sichuan border tea is kept for years and that the trade values older bricks more. It never says the bricks were made for keeping. The claims give a different reason for the make: the bricks had to survive the road and then be boiled.
